_comment: The comparison table, as DATA, because it is published in two places and a table
kept twice by hand disagrees with itself within a release. tools/comparison.mjs
writes both; frontend/tests/comparison.test.mjs fails when either drifts.
Every cell about another product is what THAT PRODUCT'S OWN page states, read on
the date below and linked from the page. Nothing here is measured by us, and
nothing is inferred: where a vendor's feature list does not mention something, the
cell says 'Not listed' rather than 'No'. The difference matters — one is a fact
about their documentation, the other is a claim about their software.
When you re-check, move 'checked' in the same edit. A date that never moves is
worse than no date, because it is believed once and then discounted.

strengths.text: The widest feature list of the four, and the only one of them sold with support: a switch port mapper, a rule engine, device snapshots, a web client and a service mode, none of which SnmpLens has. If you need one of those, this is where it is.
Part of a large suite. If you already run OpUtils or OpManager, the MIB Browser sits beside tooling you have, with one vendor answering for all of it.

Small, native Qt, packaged by several Linux distributions, and it has done the core job — browse, query, edit MIBs, receive traps — for years. If that is all you need, it is a fraction of the download.

baseline: None of these replaces Net-SNMP. `snmpwalk`, `snmpget` and `snmptrapd` are the reference implementation, they are already on the machine, and they are scriptable in a way no window is. SnmpLens is what you reach for when you want to read a MIB tree, see a table decoded by its INDEX, watch a value over time or receive a trap without writing a pipeline — not a replacement for the command line.
